title: The Oldest Share
voice_direction: Lily: calm, velvety newsreader, unhurried; a faint smile on 'isn't really a share', clipped and dry on 'Mace. Pepper. Nutmeg.', slow and quiet on the last line.
narration: The oldest share in the world was found in two thousand and ten. [pause] And it isn't really a share. It's a receipt, dated the ninth of September, sixteen-oh-six. Four years earlier, the Dutch East India Company's charter said anyone in the land could buy a share. In Amsterdam, over eleven hundred people did. Even a merchant's maid. In Enkhuizen, town messenger Pieter Harmensz put in a hundred and fifty guilders, about a year's pay, in instalments. When he paid the last one, he got this printed slip. The first dividends, from sixteen-ten, came mostly in spice. Mace. Pepper. Nutmeg. Clerks logged his payouts on the paper until sixteen-fifty. But the slip wasn't the share. A VOC share was a line in the company's ledger. To sell, you visited the company's office, where a bookkeeper moved the line to the buyer. By sixteen-eleven, Amsterdam had built a grand exchange for the trading. After Pieter died, it went into the town archive, where history student Ruben Schalk found it on his first day. It was unveiled on the ninth of September, twenty-ten: four hundred and four years to the day. Today, European law requires exchange-traded shares to be held as book entries. We've gone back to the ledger. [pause] The paper was only ever the receipt.

instagram_caption:
In 2010, a history student working in the archive at Hoorn picked up a printed form from 1606. It turned out to be the oldest known share in the world. Except it isn't quite a share.

In March 1602, the charter of the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, said that anyone living in the land could buy in. In Amsterdam alone, 1,143 people did, among them a merchant's maid with 100 guilders.

In Enkhuizen, the town messenger Pieter Harmensz put in 150 guilders, about a year's pay, in instalments. When he paid the last one, on 9 September 1606, he was given a printed receipt, filled in by hand. The first dividends, from 1610, came mostly in spice: mace, pepper, nutmeg. Clerks noted his payouts on the paper until 1650.

The paper never proved he owned anything, though. A VOC share was a line in the company's capital book, and selling one meant a trip to the East India House, where a bookkeeper moved it from one account to another.

After his death, the receipt went into the town archive. It was unveiled on 9 September 2010, 404 years to the day. Today, European law requires exchange-traded shares to be held as book entries. Back to the ledger.

Would you have bought a share in 1602? 👇

facts.claim: The Enkhuizen-chamber VOC document dated 9 September 1606 is called the world's oldest share; technically it is a receipt for the last instalment of Pieter Harmensz's 150-guilder investment
facts.source: Westfries Archief, 'The world's oldest share' / 'Het oudste aandeel'; Guinness World Records, 'Oldest share certificate'

facts.claim: Found in 2010 by Utrecht University history student Ruben Schalk while researching his MA thesis, in the Enkhuizen city archive held at the Westfries Archief in Hoorn
facts.source: Westfries Archief; Guinness World Records; Schalk, 'Financing the Dutch Golden Age: the credit market of Enkhuizen, 1580–1700' (MA, Utrecht 2010)

facts.claim: He found it by accident on his first day in the archive and noticed it because it was a printed form (printing was expensive) with details added by hand
facts.source: Bloomberg report, 2010, as summarised in press coverage (Business Standard, 'Rembrandt of shares', 18 Sep 2010)

facts.claim: It was made public on 9 September 2010 in the Westerkerk, Enkhuizen (404 years to the day after its date)
facts.source: R. Schalk, 'Leven, werk en financiën van Pieter Harmensz, de eigenaar van het oudste aandeel ter wereld' (2011); Westfries Archief

facts.claim: Pieter Harmensz was a town messenger (stadsbode) of Enkhuizen; his fixed wage was 125 guilders a year c. 1590, with colleagues earning about 200 by c. 1600 (so 150 guilders ≈ a year's pay)
Dividend payments were noted on the document up to 1650; after his death it ended up in the Enkhuizen city archive
facts.source: Westfries Archief, 'Het oudste aandeel' / 'Oudste aandeel ter wereld'

facts.claim: The VOC charter of March 1602, article 10: all residents of these lands may buy shares in this Company
facts.source: Lodewijk Petram, The World's First Stock Exchange (Columbia UP, 2014); 'The world's first IPO'

facts.claim: Amsterdam subscription closed 31 August 1602 with 1,143 investors; held at the house of director Dirck van Os, whose maid Neeltgen Cornelis subscribed 100 guilders
facts.source: Petram, 'The world's first IPO'; Petram, PhD thesis (UvA 2011)

facts.claim: From 1610 the VOC paid a series of dividends mostly in kind: mace (75% of nominal), pepper (50%), and nutmeg (30%, declared March 1612); only small cash portions
facts.source: Gelderblom, de Jong & Jonker, 'The VOC insurance contract of 1613' (Yale/UU working paper; European Review of Economic History 24:2)

facts.claim: The VOC issued no bearer shares; ownership was a positive balance in the capital book, and transfers required buyer and seller at the East India House, where the bookkeeper moved the share after two directors approved
facts.source: Petram, PhD thesis 'The world's first stock exchange: how the Amsterdam market for Dutch East India Company shares became a modern securities market, 1602–1700' (UvA 2011)

facts.claim: Hendrick de Keyser's exchange building on the Rokin, Amsterdam, was completed in 1611; VOC shares were traded there
facts.source: Beursgeschiedenis.nl (Exchange History), 'The exchange of Hendrick de Keyser'

facts.claim: EU CSDR Article 3: securities admitted to trading or traded on trading venues must be in book-entry form; applies to all such transferable securities from 1 January 2025
facts.source: ESMA Interactive Single Rulebook, CSDR Art. 3; Banque de France
